title: Side effects of 58 years of copper sulfate treatment of the Fairmont Lakes, Minnesota
venue: JAWRA Journal of the American Water Resources Association (Water Resources Bulletin)
dose: copper sulfate, cumulative up to 1,647 kg/ha; 1.5 million kg total
result: Treatments killed algae temporarily, but populations recovered within 7-21 days; long-term, algae became more copper-tolerant and species shifted from green to blue-green algae.
env_effects: Oxygen depletion, faster phosphorus recycling from sediment, occasional fish kills, copper accumulation in sediments, shift from game to rough fish, loss of macrophytes and fewer benthic invertebrates.

title: Occurrence of copper resistant mutants in the toxic cyanobacteria Microcystis aeruginosa: characterisation and future implications in the use of copper sulphate as algaecide
authors: Garcia-Villada L, Rico M, Altamirano MM, Sanchez-Martin L, Lopez-Rodas V, Costas E
scale: Modified Luria-Delbrück fluctuation analysis: 198 set-1 and 198 set-2 replicate cultures of M. aeruginosa strain MaM1, plus fitness dose-response (n = 3)
dose: 10 µM free Cu2+ for selection; fitness tested across 1-10.5 µM Cu2+
duration: About 4 weeks to 1 month under copper for resistant cells to regrow
result: 10 µM Cu2+ destroyed sensitive cells within days, but 32 of 198 set-1 cultures (and all 198 set-2 cultures) regrew from rare copper-resistant cells; the spontaneous mutation rate was 1.76x10^-6 mutants per cell division. Wild-type fitness fell to zero at 3.2-10.5 µM Cu2+, where resistant mutants grew best.
env_effects: Resistant mutants were smaller and less fit without copper; authors warn repeated copper treatment of water supplies selects for resistance.
key_details: Lab fluctuation analysis distinguishing pre-existing spontaneous mutations from induced adaptation: set-1 variance/mean was >50 (set 2 ~1), showing resistance arises randomly before copper exposure. Repeatability 96%, reproducibility 100%. Without copper, resistant mutants had 20% lower Malthusian fitness and were smaller (3.99 vs 4.54 µm diameter). Authors conclude repeated copper sulphate dosing of supply reservoirs can select persistent resistant toxic populations. Single strain, lab only.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record's 'above 5.8 µM' threshold was not found in the full text; the results give wild-type fitness zero and resistant fitness maximal at 3.2-10.5 µM Cu2+.

title: Effect of copper sulphate treatment on natural phytoplanktonic communities
authors: Le Jeune AH, Charpin M, Deluchat V, Briand JF, Lenain JF, Baudu M, Amblard C
scale: Nine 85 L indoor glass aquaria filled with Lake Pontalage (France) water, 200 µm-screened; triplicate controls, 80 and 160 µg Cu/L; run separately in spring and summer 2004
dose: 80 and 160 ug Cu/L (below and above complexation capacity)
result: Biomass fell until day 5 (80 µg/L) or day 8 (160 µg/L), then regrew; in summer, biomass stayed significantly below controls from day 12 to 27 at 80 µg/L and until day 27 at 160 µg/L, while in spring the 80 µg/L treatment ended higher than controls (days 16-20). Cyanobacteria biomass was significantly lower than controls at both doses in both seasons (p < 0.001), but cyanobacteria were at low density (7.5% of summer biomass) with no bloom present.
env_effects: 160 µg/L gave Chlorophyceae dominance (>85% of biomass) and nanophytoplankton >90% of biomass, with microphytoplankton significantly suppressed; diatoms, Chrysophyceae and Cryptophyceae (spring) also reduced. The lake had never been treated with algicide.
key_details: Replicated (n = 3) indoor mesocosm test of copper sulphate on natural phytoplankton sampled before any bloom formed; no nutrients added, zooplankton >200 µm removed. In untreated controls cyanobacteria rose to 40% (spring) and 30% (summer) of biomass, while copper significantly suppressed them at both doses. Total biomass responses were season-dependent. Because the starting community had low cyanobacteria and no bloom, this tests preventive dosing rather than bloom control.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record says total biomass 'recovered within a few days'; it declined for 5-8 days, and in summer stayed significantly below controls for most of the 27 days. Record omits that no bloom was present (cyanobacteria ~7.5% of summer biomass) and the 85 L, n = 3 design.

title: Cellular and aqueous microcystin-LR following laboratory exposures of Microcystis aeruginosa to copper algaecides
authors: Iwinski KJ, Calomeni AJ, Geer TD, Rodgers JH
result: Cellular MC-LR and chlorophyll-a declined with copper (sigmoidal exposure-response) and total MC-LR fell below untreated controls, but aqueous MC-LR rose with copper concentration; CuSO4 gave 10-20% more aqueous and total MC-LR than copper-ethanolamine at 0.5-1.0 mg Cu/L.
env_effects: Toxin moves from cells into the water; lower copper doses were as effective while releasing less toxin.

title: Laboratory-scale evaluation of algaecide effectiveness for control of microcystin-producing cyanobacteria from Lake Okeechobee, Florida (USA)
authors: Kinley-Baird C, Calomeni A, Berthold DE, Lefler FW, Barbosa M, Rodgers JH, Laughinghouse HD
organism: Lake Okeechobee cyanobacterial assemblage (6.14 x 10^6 cells/mL; 71% Microcystis aeruginosa, 29% Pseudanabaena mucicola)
scale: 200 mL site water in 400 mL beakers, n=3 per concentration, 4 label-range concentrations per product
dose: Minimum effective measured exposures: SeClear (copper sulfate) 0.51 mg Cu/L; chelated Cu (Algimycin PWF, Argos, Captain XTR, Cutrine Ultra) 0.63-0.74 mg Cu/L; GreenClean Liquid 5.0 11.4 mg H2O2/L; GreenClean Liquid 5.0 11.8 mg H2O2/L + Hydrothol 191 0.198 mg endothall acid/L
duration: responses 3 days after treatment; toxins at 1, 4, 9 days
result: At minimum effective doses, chelated copper cut cell density 77-90% and SeClear and GreenClean Liquid 5.0 (alone or with Hydrothol 191) >90-95% versus untreated controls at 3 days; granular peroxides (GreenClean Pro, PAK 27, Phycomycin SCP) and Hydrothol 191 alone achieved only 34-48%. Chelated copper kept most microcystin cell-bound at day 1 (10-23% aqueous vs 79-99% for SeClear and peroxide), and total microcystin fell below 10 ug/L by day 9 in all copper treatments.
env_effects: Short-term toxin release; authors call for larger-scale studies before use.
key_details: Lab exposures of Lake Okeechobee water collected August 7, 2019, with 10 USEPA-registered algaecides plus one combination, each at 4 label-range concentrations (n=3), and untreated controls (n=3). Controls grew from 6.14 to 8.06 x 10^6 cells/mL over 3 days. Cell density, chlorophyll-a and phycocyanin were measured 3 days after treatment; microcystin (cellular vs aqueous) at 1, 4 and 9 days. Control total microcystin was 787 ug/L at day 1 and 547 ug/L at day 9; by day 4, Algimycin PWF, Argos and Captain XTR treatments were at 11-28 ug/L. Measured peroxide and endothall exposures were 38% and 41% off target, so results use measured concentrations. Bench scale only.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record lists SeClear as a non-copper product; it is copper sulfate-based (0.51 mg Cu/L) and released 91% of microcystin into water at day 1. Granular peroxide products and Hydrothol 191 alone were only 34-48% effective, which the record omits.

title: Treatment of the red tide dinoflagellate Karenia brevis and brevetoxins using USEPA-registered algaecides
authors: Hu J, Berthold DE, Wang Y, Xiao X, Laughinghouse HD
dose: three copper algaecides (from 0.31-0.34 mg Cu/L) and three peroxide algaecides (4.89-7.08 mg H2O2/L)
result: As little as 0.31-0.34 mg Cu/L significantly decreased K. brevis cells within 24 h; brevetoxin at 72 h fell most with 1.00 mg Cu/L Algimycin PWF and the higher peroxide doses.
env_effects: Fate of copper and toxins and effects on marine non-target species not tested; authors say pilot studies on marine non-targets are needed before use.

title: New is not always better: Toxicity of novel copper based algaecides to Daphnia magna
authors: Kang L, Mucci M, Fang J, Lurling M
dose: Measured-stock dilutions of CuSO4.5H2O, Captain XTR, SeClear and Lake Guard Blue; chronic top doses set at the acute EC10 (about 0.4-0.5 mg Cu/L)
result: Acute 48 h EC50s ranged 0.50 (Lake Guard Blue) to 0.60 (Captain XTR) mg Cu/L (CuSO4 0.521). In 21 d tests the top doses (0.4-0.5 mg Cu/L) cut population growth rate by 29% (CuSO4), 49% (Captain XTR), 48% (SeClear) and 37% (Lake Guard Blue), and SeClear's top dose left only 60% survival.
env_effects: All four products cut Daphnia reproduction and growth at 0.4-0.5 mg Cu/L, below the USEPA-allowed 1 mg Cu/L (about twice the acute EC50). Test medium contained EDTA, which chelated most copper, so field toxicity could differ.
key_details: Lab ecotoxicity on Daphnia magna only (no algae treated). Acute tests: triplicates of five neonates per concentration, 48 h immobility. Chronic tests: 10 single-animal replicates per concentration for 21 days, fed Scenedesmus; stock Cu verified by ICP-OES. First brood was delayed 1.8-3.2 days at the highest doses; reproduction EC50s 0.274 (SeClear) to 0.498 (Captain XTR) mg Cu/L. Authors still see copper as an emergency option where nutrient control is absent.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record is correct; adds that effects occur at about half the US label maximum (1 mg Cu/L) and the EDTA-medium caveat.

title: A critical review on operation and performance of source water control strategies for cyanobacterial blooms: Part I-chemical control methods
authors: Kibuye FA, Zamyadi A, Wert EC
result: Review of in-lake chemical controls (Al, Fe, lanthanum-modified bentonite, Ca, H2O2, Cu, KMnO4) finds that algaecides act fast but blooms rebound; one site needed up to six monthly copper applications with an average rebound time of 14 days. The authors conclude no single chemical strategy is a complete solution and external nutrient reduction is fundamental.
env_effects: Over 90% of applied copper transfers to sediments; high mortality of fish and other fauna after Cu treatment has been linked to oxygen depletion or high doses. A whole-creek 50 mg/L H2O2 treatment cut zooplankton by 99% after 50 h, raised NH4+ 97%, and caused some fish kills.
key_details: Narrative critical review with tables of field and pilot-scale studies covering nutrient-inactivation agents and algaecides. Copper examples: >90% chlorophyll-a decline at 0.02-1 mg/L Cu at low/medium Microcystis densities but higher doses needed at 10^7 cells/mL; an Albay et al. (2003) Microcystis bloom rebounded despite daily Cu dosing under high nutrient inputs. H2O2 examples: 99% cell decline 10 days after whole-lake injection, with cells back to 2 x 10^5 cells/mL at 49 days; 99% A. ostenfeldii decline in 48 h with 50 mg/L H2O2. It also covers toxin release, dose timing and US regulations.

title: Occurrence of toxic cyanobacteria before and after copper sulphate treatment in a water reservoir, Istanbul, Turkey
authors: Albay M, Akcaalan R, Aykulu G, Tufekci H, Beattie KA, Codd GA
dose: CuSO4 to surface water: 1,600 kg (Apr 2000), 4,800 kg (May), 5,050 kg (Jun), 5,000 kg (Jul), then 800 kg in Sep
result: M. aeruginosa bloomed again whenever treatment stopped (78.91 mg/L surface biomass on 20 Sep 2000); 800 kg of CuSO4 then cut surface biomass to 34.75 mg/L, a 3.1-fold decrease reported at the surface.
env_effects: Tonnes of copper added to a drinking-water reservoir; total nitrogen increased slightly after treatment; microcystin was present in the bloom (2.1 ug/L in raw water in 1999).

title: The effects of three chemical algaecides on cell numbers and toxin content of the cyanobacteria Microcystis aeruginosa and Anabaenopsis sp.
authors: Greenfield DI, Duquette A, Goodson A, Keppler CJ, Williams SH, Brock LM, Stackley KD, White D, Wilde SB
organism: Microcystis aeruginosa (culture, 5 psu) and Anabaenopsis sp. bloom water (21 psu) from a brackish stormwater pond
scale: 1 L flasks in triplicate per algaecide x dose, starting at ~5x10^5 cells/mL
dose: Captain (chelated copper carbonate; label 0.4 ppm), K-Tea (copper-triethanolamine; label 0.5 ppm) and Pak 27 (85% sodium percarbonate; label 6.5 lb/acre-ft), each at 0.5x, 1x and 2x label dose
result: After 7 days, both copper algaecides left significantly fewer cells than Pak 27 or controls at 1x and 2x (and for Anabaenopsis at all doses); Captain at 0.5x did not differ from control, and 0.5x Pak 27 cells were slightly more than double. Total microcystin (initially 11-30 ppb) generally rose over the experiments, often ending 2-10x above initial, with toxin shifting to the dissolved phase.
env_effects: Algaecides may visibly control a bloom without reducing toxin, a public-health concern.
key_details: Lab flask exposures (n = 3) of three commercial algaecides at half, label and double doses, sampled at 4, 8, 24, 48, 72 h and 7 days. Toxin analysis was done only for the M. aeruginosa culture because the Anabaenopsis bloom had microcystin <0.1 ppb. The copper products controlled cell numbers but no product reduced overall toxin; particulate:dissolved microcystin ratios dropped, meaning toxin moved into the water. The percarbonate product was the least effective on cell numbers.
fulltext_discrepancy: Record omits that total microcystin often increased 2-10x above initial during the experiments, and that toxin results come from the culture only (bloom water had <0.1 ppb).

title: Evaluation of algaecide effectiveness of five different oxidants applied on harmful phytoplankton
authors: Moreno-Andres J, Romero-Martinez L, Seoane S, Acevedo-Merino A, Moreno-Garrido I, Nebot E
dose: peracetic acid, peroxymonosulfate, peroxydisulfate, H2O2, chlorine
result: Peracetic acid (EC50 0.32-2.70 mg/L) and peroxymonosulfate (EC50 0.40-1.99 mg/L) acted strongly but briefly, H2O2 (EC50 6.67-7.08 mg/L) gave a sustained effect, and peroxydisulfate was negligible.
env_effects: Not assessed; PAA, PMS or H2O2 proposed as alternatives to chlorine-based reagents.

title: Oxidation of Microcystis aeruginosa and microcystins with peracetic acid
authors: Alnahas M, Almuhtaram H, Hofmann R
dose: peracetic acid 10 mg/L (with ~10% H2O2 in the product)
result: At acidic pH, 10 mg/L PAA damaged cells immediately and killed them in 15-60 min, but at neutral and alkaline pH death came only after a 3-6 h lag; toxin degradation rates were orders of magnitude below free chlorine. Authors judge PAA impractically slow for cell or microcystin control.
env_effects: Slow lysis: <35% of intracellular MC-LR was in solution after 12 h at 10 mg/L, so low risk of sudden toxin release.
